suggestions.assertion: OUTPUT_DIR/pr-body.md exists, and its problem section opens with one sentence of at most 20 words ...
suggestions.reason: The lede landed at exactly 20 words, and the longest body sentences at exactly 25. The run is clearly steering to the limit rather than well under it; the assertion still discriminates, but the author may want to know the skill produces boundary-hugging prose rather than short prose.

No assertion checks that the PR body's technical claims about the diff are true (Retry-After uncapped, jitter default 0.0, FixedWindowLimiter removed from __init__). A body that invents reviewer-facing caveats would pass every current assertion. A check that each named parameter/default exists in the committed source would make the 'details a reviewer should weigh' section hard to fake.

The test-before-push assertion is graded from a transcript summary line. The && chain is good evidence here, but a transcript that merely said 'tests passed' would be indistinguishable from an unread result. Having the executor record the raw make test tail in the transcript would make this verifiable rather than trusted.

eval_feedback.overall: Clean run, 15/15. Assertions are well targeted at structure and prose mechanics; the gap is correctness of the body's statements about the code, which nothing checks.

notes: All 15 assertions pass on reproduced evidence (check_run.py, both prose-lint runs, git inspection, make test rerun). Two things worth the eval author's attention: the writing hugs the limits exactly (20-word lede, 25-word sentences), so the thresholds are doing work but the skill is optimizing to them rather than below them; and no assertion verifies the PR body's claims about the code itself (uncapped Retry-After, jitter default, removed export), so a body that fabricated plausible caveats would also score 15/15. The test-before-push assertion rests on the transcript's '&&' chain rather than a captured test result; still convincing here, but a looser transcript would make it untestable.
